facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Decca Records Rejection (Pre-1964)
facts.body: The band was famously rejected by at least one record label, Decca, whose executives felt that "guitar groups were on the way out" and that "The Beatles have no future in show business." "A band famously rejected by at least one record label, Deca, because they felt that guitar groups were on the way out."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
facts.body: The Beatles' appearance on Ed Sullivan in February 1964 inspired countless people to form bands, significantly changing music across all genres within just seven years. Despite their breakup in 1970, they are still regarded as the most influential rock group of all time. "how many stories have you heard about people deciding to form a band after seeing the Beatles on Ants Sullivan in February 1964?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Ed Sullivan Performance - John Cummings' Inspiration (1964)
facts.body: John Cummings (later Johnny Ramone) was deeply influenced by seeing The Beatles perform on The Ed Sullivan Show in 1964, sparking his love for the guitar. "He had been in love with the guitar ever since he saw the Beatles' plan Ed Sullivan back in 1964."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
facts.body: Their legendary appearance on the Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964, marked the beginning of rock's second cycle. This event "rescued Rock" and created a "tsunami that spread across the planet," influencing music for the remainder of the 1960s. "Cycle 2 starts 13 years later with the American TV debut The Beatles on the Ed Sullivan Show, February 9th, 1964."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Extreme Conditions at Toronto Concert (1964)
facts.body: The atmosphere inside Maple Leaf Gardens on September 6, 1964, was intensely hot and muggy, with temperatures around 30 degrees Celsius outside and even higher inside. Soda and ice cream vendors ran out of supplies, and water fountains barely functioned, yet the fervent fans' dehydration and exhaustion were no match for their enthusiasm. "It was a hot, muggy, late summer day with temperatures at around 30 degrees Celsius. Inside the venue it was even hotter, and soda and ice cream vendors were running out."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: First North American Tour Stop in Winnipeg (1964)
facts.body: On a warm, cloudy day in mid-August 1964, The Beatles were flying from London to San Francisco for their inaugural major North American tour, making an unplanned refueling stop in Winnipeg. This stop unexpectedly turned into a major event when CJAYTV's Bob Burns announced their arrival on local radio, leading to the airport being swarmed by frenzied fans. "The band landed on August 18, 1964 at 2.5pm."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: First Official Canadian Performance in Vancouver (1964)
facts.body: The Beatles' first official Canadian concert and performance took place on August 22, 1964, at the Pacific National Exhibition (PNE) in Vancouver, British Columbia. The PNE is an annual 15-day summer fair and amusement park. "And the concert was held at the Pacific National Exhibition in Vancouver, British Columbia."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Friendship with The Ronettes (1964)
facts.body: During The Ronettes' brief UK tour in early 1964, they became friendly with The Beatles. Ronnie had a "brief chaste flirtation" with John Lennon, and Estelle had a "little more" with George Harrison. "they became friendly with the Beatles, Ronnie had a brief chaste flirtation with John Lennon, and Estelle something a little more with George Harrison."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 110: "Be My Baby" by the Ronettes
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Hotel Invasion by Fans (1964)
facts.body: During The Beatles' stay at the King Edward Hotel in Toronto in September 1964, teens relentlessly bypassed security, creating an "infestation" for which the hotel seemed to have "no repellent." At 3 am, radio journalist Larry Cain, traveling with the band, encountered a teen in an oversized housekeeping uniform knocking on his door, asking for soap and then if he could take her to The Beatles. "Teens kept getting past security. It was as if the hotel was dealing with an infestation for which they had no repellent."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Identical Second Toronto Concert (1964)
facts.body: The Beatles' second concert at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto, which began at 10 pm on September 6, 1964, was virtually identical to the first. It featured screaming fans, blinding flash bulbs, raining lipsticks and bras, resulting in continued frenzy and fainting among the audience, echoing the "mass hysteria" of the earlier show. "If you've seen footage from a Beatles concert, you can imagine that the second concert was identical to the first."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
facts.body: The Beatles' debut performance on The Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964, is considered a watershed moment that irrevocably changed rock and roll forever. This pivotal event, which profoundly reshaped music history, might not have happened had Sullivan's flight not been delayed and if The Beatles had not coincidentally been at Heathrow Airport at the same time.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Impact on Guitar Band Demand (1964)
facts.body: Following The Beatles' arrival in America in February 1964, there was an unprecedented surge in demand for electric guitars, as countless aspiring musicians were inspired to form guitar bands. This event marked a significant turning point in the popularity of the electric guitar. "After the Beatles hit America in February 1964, everyone wanted to be in a guitar band. Demand for new instruments exploded."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: John Lennon's Clash with Red Robinson (1964)
facts.body: Halfway through the Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, as the crowd neared rioting, local radio host Red Robinson was instructed to go on stage to calm the fans. John Lennon, unaware of the situation, confronted Robinson, telling him, "Get off our stage, nobody interrupts the Beatles," before relenting after Robinson explained that manager Brian Epstein had sent him. "John looked down at Brian Epstein, the band's manager who gave him the okay. John turned Robinson and said, Okay, carry on mate."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: King Edward Hotel Frenzy (1964)
facts.body: Upon their arrival at the King Edward Hotel in downtown Toronto on September 6, 1964, a frenzy of fans greeted The Beatles, leading to Paul McCartney having his shirt torn and Ringo Starr being separated from John and George. Although police quickly restored order on the street, Beatlemania continued inside, where a 14-year-old girl was found hiding in the linen closet of their royal suite. "Paul would have a shirt torn open by a fan, wrangle with separated from John and George, but thankfully police were able to quickly restore order on the street and get the band into the hotel."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Mass Hysteria at Maple Leaf Gardens (1964)
facts.body: Upon The Beatles' appearance on stage at Maple Leaf Gardens on September 6, 1964, flash bulbs went off, blinding everyone, and the roar of 16,761 screaming voices made it impossible to hear the music, blinding and deafening the band. Items like bras and lipsticks rained down, leading to 109 fans fainting at the venue, described as "mass hysteria" rather than just a rock show. "It's unclear if they could even hear their own voices over the roar of 16,761 streaming voices, nor do we know if they could see anything as bras, lipsticks, and other items rain down on them."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Massive Police Deployment in Toronto (1964)
facts.body: The Beatles' first visit to Toronto in September 1964 necessitated an extraordinary police response, with more than 850 officers from the city, the Ontario Provincial Police, and the counties called in. By noon, 4,000 police officers and auxiliaries were on duty around Maple Leaf Gardens, dividing the crowd into smaller sections, with majestic horses used to push back waves of "deranged youth." "The band's first visit to Toronto required more than 850 officers from the city, the Ontario provincial police, and the counties."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Mayor Phil Givens Snubbed (1964)
facts.body: On September 6, 1964, Toronto mayor Phil Givens and his wife attempted to visit The Beatles at the King Edward Hotel at 1:30 pm but were turned away by a "blonde woman." She claimed two of the Beatles were sleeping and two were with relatives, an incident that led to the Daily Star publishing an article with the headline, "Beatles Blonde, Snob is Mayor." "The next day, the daily star released an article with the headline, Beatles Blonde, Snob is Mayor."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Montreal Arrival and Death Threats (1964)
facts.body: The Beatles' arrival at Dorval Airport for their only visit to La Belle province mirrored the scenes at other tour stops, with hordes of screaming fans. However, their time in Quebec was significantly marred by death threats from French Canadian separatists, specifically the FLQ, leading to the presence of police sharpshooters at the Montreal Forum on St. Catherine Street for their two concerts. "Their arrival at the Dorval Airport mirrored what happened at every stop on their tour. Hordes of screaming fans at the airport throngs of fans lying the streets, clutching magazines and singing their favorite Beatles songs."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Opening Acts Booed by Impatient Crowd (1964)
facts.body: At the Maple Leaf Gardens concert in Toronto on September 6, 1964, the opening bands, which included Bill Black's Combo, The Exciters, Clarence "Frogman" Henry, and Jackie De Shannon, were met with boos from the crowd. The audience was impatient and made it clear they wanted only one band: The Beatles. "As the opening bands, which included Bill Black's combo, the exciders Clarence Frogman Henry, and the Celterie Jackie De Shannon hit the stage to crowd-bood, they only wanted one band, and one band only."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Pan Am Flight 101 Arrival - February 7, 1964
facts.body: The band's arrival on Pan Am Flight 101 from London at JFK Airport in New York on February 7, 1964, symbolized a massive explosion of Britishness and national pride. This event was referenced as a benchmark for the level of national pride seen again during the Britpop era. "an explosion of pride in Britishness that we really hadn't seen since February 7, 1964 when Pan Am Flight 101 from London touched down at JFK Airport in New York carrying a band called The Beatles."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Paul McCartney Greets Winnipeg (1964)
facts.body: Following the incident with Bryce Decker at the Winnipeg airport on August 18, 1964, Paul McCartney exited the plane, yelled "Hello, Winnipeg," and descended the stairs, where he was immediately swarmed by a throng of reporters, including Bob Burns. This brief appearance was the band's only direct interaction with the Winnipeg crowd, as they never returned to the city. "Oh, and the man who greeted the crowd was none other than Paul McCartney."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Peaceful Departure from Toronto (1964)
facts.body: The day after their chaotic concerts, just before noon on September 7, 1964, The Beatles headed back to the Toronto airport. The sun was shining, the crowd was considerably smaller than the previous day, and the mood was distinctly different. The band signed autographs, posed for photos, waved to their admirers, and then boarded their plane, marking the end of their first Toronto visit. "The sun was shining, and the crowd was considerably smaller. The mood was also different. This was the end."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Post-Concert Activities and Press Conference (1964)
facts.body: After their first concert at Maple Leaf Gardens ended around 6 pm on September 6, 1964, The Beatles were quickly moved to a dressing room. There, they took photographs with local DJs, fan club presidents, and Miss Canada, followed by a press conference where they appeared somewhat bewildered but maintained their charming demeanor and "savage wit" towards journalists. "They then had a press conference where they looked a little bewildered, but as usual they were charming to admirers, and unleashed their savage wit on journalists."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Beatles

facts.title: Ringo Starr's Worry Over Montreal Threats (1964)
facts.body: Ringo Starr expressed genuine worry about the death threats received during The Beatles' 1964 Montreal concerts. He recalled that some individuals targeted him "as an English Jew," despite him not being Jewish, noting that while threats were often taken "in stride," this particular incident, despite more police presence, was one of the few times he was truly concerned. "Some people decided to make an example of me as an English Jew. The one major fault is, I'm not Jewish. Threats we took in stride. I mean, suddenly there'd be a few more cops, but this was one of the few times I was really worried."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Origins and Original Era (1964-1968)

An estimated 184,000 Garage bands formed in the US during those four years alone. "The roots of Garage Rock began in the early 1960s, when bands inspired by the Beatles and the rest of the British invasion started springing up like mushrooms."

facts.title: Brian Wilson's Mental Breakdown (December 1964)
facts.body: The extreme mental strain caused by constant touring finally led to Brian Wilson suffering a breakdown in December 1964 while on a plane to Texas, where he was heard screaming and refused to disembark. Although he managed to perform that night's show, he immediately flew back to Los Angeles, effectively retiring from the road. Glenn Campbell was subsequently brought in to replace him on stage for the next five months. "The mental strain of touring had finally got too much for Brian, and in December, on a plane to Texas, he'd had a breakdown, screaming on the plane and refusing to get off."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Brian Wilson's Production Style Evolution (1964)
facts.body: As recording sessions progressed in 1964, Brian Wilson's artistic ambition significantly increased, evident in his focus on the emotional impact of the music and the complexity of his arrangements. He increasingly employed session musicians to augment the group's sound and developed a distinctive production style. This style was a variation of Phil Spector's "Wall of Sound," but one that prioritized "gentle fragility" over Spector's characteristic "storm and drang." "As these recordings progressed, Brian Wilson was more and more ambitious, both in terms of the emotional effect of the music and his arrangements, increasingly using session musicians to augment the group, and trying for a variance of full spectre's production style, but one which emphasised gentle fragility rather than storm and drang."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Re-purposing Girl Group Style (1964)
facts.body: In songs such as "Don't Worry Baby," Brian Wilson demonstrated a unique ability to adapt the emotional and musical aesthetics of girl group songs to explore themes of emotional vulnerability. This approach often delved into acknowledging and processing aspects of what is now termed "toxic masculinity," a subject rarely tackled in music of that era. "This repurposing of the emotional and musical style of girl group songs, to deal with the emotional vulnerability that comes from acknowledging and attempting to process toxic masculinity, is something that few other songwriters were capable of at this point."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

"Possibly the greatest track he created in 1964 ended up not being used by The Beach Boys, though, but was given to Glenn Campbell."

facts.title: Post-Prison Commercial Resurgence (1964)
facts.body: Serving 18 months in jail unexpectedly revitalized Chuck Berry's commercial prospects. Upon his release in 1964, his first three singles—"Nadine," "You Never Can Tell," and "No Particular Place To Go"—were all bigger hits than he had experienced since 1958, suggesting a potential return to the top. "As odd as it is to say, Barry's 18 months in jail may have done him some good as a commercial prospect."

facts.title: Studio Work Decline After 1964
facts.body: Following a brief commercial resurgence in 1964, Chuck Berry's studio recordings largely reverted to mediocrity, marked by only occasional flashes of his earlier brilliance. This period saw a general decline in the quality of his new music. "But it was a false dawn. Barry's studio works slid back into mediocrity with occasional flashes of his old brilliance."

facts.title: Personal Tragedies (1964-1968)
facts.body: The period following 1964 was marked by severe personal tragedies for Roy Orbison. He divorced his wife Claudette in November 1964 due to her infidelity, though they reconciled and remarried in December 1965. Just six months later, in June 1966, Claudette died in a motorcycle accident. A little over two years after that, while Orbison was on tour in the UK, his house burned down, killing two of his three children. "The events of the next few years were the kind of thing that would break almost anyone."

facts.title: Dave Richmond's Departure and Tom McGuinness's Arrival (1964)
facts.body: Dave Richmond was seen as a "great jazz bass player" who wanted to emulate Charles Mingus, playing "strange cross-rhythms." The group needed someone to play "straightforward blues bass lines without complaint," closer to Willie Dixon. Tom McGuinness, a guitarist who bluffed his way into the bass player role, replaced Richmond. McGuinness had never played bass before his first gig and was only asked if he was willing to play simple parts during his interview. "Richmond was a great bass player, but he was a great jazz bass player. He wanted to be Charles Mingus, and play strange cross-vethams, and what the group needed at this point was someone who would just play straightforward blues bass lines without complaint, they needed someone closer to Willie Dixon than to Mingus."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.name: Manfred Mann

facts.title: Miserable American Tour (1964)
facts.body: After the success of "Doo Wah Diddy Diddy," the group embarked on an American tour packaged with Peter and Gordon. The experience proved "thoroughly miserable," leading the group to decide against returning to the US, resulting in only minor successes there for the rest of the decade, despite continued hits in Britain. "The group found the experience of touring the US, a thoroughly miserable one, and decided that they weren't going to bother going back again."

facts.name: Manfred Mann

facts.title: Temporary Replacement for Brian Wilson (December 1964 - Five Months)
facts.body: Glenn Campbell, an accomplished session guitarist who had contributed to several Beach Boys recordings and had a nascent singing career, swiftly stepped in to replace Brian Wilson on stage for five months following Wilson's mental breakdown in December 1964. Campbell performed most of the group's live shows during this period. "Campbell, who was a session guitarist who had played on a number of The Beach Boys recordings, had had a minor career as a singer at this point, had flown out at almost no notice, and for the next five months he replaced Brian on stage for most of their shows, before the group got a permanent replacement in."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Received Beach Boys Track (1964)
facts.body: Glenn Campbell was given what was possibly Brian Wilson's greatest track composed in 1964, a song that The Beach Boys ultimately did not use themselves. This was offered as a significant favor, acknowledging Campbell's invaluable service as a temporary touring replacement for Brian Wilson after his breakdown. "Possibly the greatest track he created in 1964 ended up not being used by The Beach Boys, though, but was given to Glenn Campbell."

facts.title: Intentional Speaker Damage for Distortion (1964)
facts.body: Dave Davies was an early pioneer in physically modifying amplifiers to achieve distortion. In 1964, while recording a song with The Kinks, he intentionally damaged the speaker cone of his small amplifier, using either a razor blade or a screwdriver, to produce a distorted sound. While effective in creating the desired effect, this method offered little control over the specific type or intensity of the distortion. "When the band was recording this song in 1964, he slashed the speaker cone of his small amp."

facts.body: Often cited as the first heavy metal record, this song introduced heavily distorted guitar riffs to the top of the UK charts. Ray Davis developed the basic melody years earlier, evolving from a jazz piano piece (inspired by Jerry Mulligan's "Jazz On A Summer's Day") to a Chet Atkins-style instrumental, and then a Mose Allison-style piece. Its final form was heavily influenced by Larry Page, who suggested focusing on riffs due to Ray's singing, pointing to The Kingsmen's "Louie Louie" as inspiration, and changing the opening lyric from "yeah" to "girl" for audience connection and to address subtle questions about the group's sexuality. The defining distorted sound came from Dave Davis, who slashed his amplifier cone with a knife and fed the sound through a larger amp, a technique almost unknown in Britain at the time that helped standardize fuzz guitar in rock. The original recording was overproduced by Shell Tauhmey with excessive echo and a Phil Spector-like sound, which Ray despised. Larry Page, leveraging his publishing rights with Eddie Casna, insisted on a re-recording, which Robert Wace funded. The second take of the re-recording session, featuring Bobby Graham on drums and Arthur Greenslade on piano, was deemed "extraordinary" and captured Dave Davis's iconic solo, despite Ray's excited "oh no" mid-take. Released on August 4, 1964, it became a smash hit, reaching number one in the UK in September and the Top 10 in the US. "You really got me was released on the 4th of August 1964, and became a smash hit, reaching number one in September."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Two months before The Beatles' "I Feel Fine" was recorded, The Kinks were working at IBC Studios in London. Frustrated with not achieving the desired sound for a song Ray Davies had written on piano, his brother Dave Davies took a razor blade to the speaker cone of his Vox Elpico amp and poked holes in it with a pin. This deliberate damage created a cool, distorted sound that became iconic for the track. "But not before Brother Dave Davies hacked up the speaker code of his Vox Elpico amp with a razor blade and poking some holes in it with a pin for good measure."
